Ultrasound duplex scan of the right upper quadrant and biliary tree.

The liver measures 14.8 cm in craniocaudal dimension, demonstrating normal
parenchymal echogenicity without focal mass or hepatic surface nodularity.
Main portal vein is patent with hepatopetal flow at 22 cm/s.

The gallbladder is distended with mild diffuse wall thickening measuring
3.8 mm (normal less than 3 mm). Several mobile, shadowing, hyperechoic

hydronephrosis or calculi. Spleen is normal in size, measuring 10.4 cm.

Dr. [presidio-person], [presidio-location]
Staff Radiologist, Calloway Regional Hospital

From: the patient
To: the diabetes and rheumatology care team
Subject: ankle swelling on the steroid taper

hi team, this is the patient. i am a [presidio-date-time] and my daughter has been lining up the pill box since the flare that started after i was diagnosed in [presidio-date-time]. the hands have been stiffer since [presidio-date-time], and recently the left ankle blew up so i could not get a shoe on. the home cuff [presidio-date-time] showed blood pressure 148/92 mmHg, pulse 96 beats per minute, and weight 71.4 kg. medicines i took: methotrexate 15 mg PO once [presidio-date-time], folic acid 1 mg PO [presidio-date-time], metformin 500 mg PO BID, and Allegra 180 mg PO [presidio-date-time] for the allergies. the taper card says prednisone 40/30/20/10 mg PO [presidio-date-time], [presidio-date-time] on each dose, and i am in the middle of the 30 mg step. i did not take the tramadol. please tell me if i should come in or just wait on labs. my daughter can read the reply with me [presidio-date-time].

From: the covering pharmacist
To: the patient
Subject: re: ankle swelling on the steroid taper

Thank you for writing this out so clearly. We compared your note with the records that arrived from Outside Hospital and with the bloodwork drawn at the clinic.

Past Medical History: seropositive rheumatoid arthritis, seasonal allergic rhinitis, prediabetes, and a remote Bell palsy that resolved without residual weakness.

Medications to continue: methotrexate 15 mg PO once [presidio-date-time], folic acid 1 mg PO [presidio-date-time], metformin 500 mg PO BID, and Allegra 180 mg PO [presidio-date-time]. Stay on the written taper, prednisone 40/30/20/10 mg PO [presidio-date-time], and do not skip a step or go backward unless we tell you to. For pain use acetaminophen 650 mg PO q6h PRN, limit 3 g in [presidio-date-time]. Hold tramadol 50 mg PO q6h PRN unless the pain is severe and the ankle is not hot or red.

Labs from the clinic visit: creatinine 0.9 mg/dL, eGFR 78 mL/min/1.73 [presidio-us-driver-license], ESR 42 mm/hr, CRP 1.8 mg/dL, hemoglobin 11.6 g/dL, potassium 4.1 mmol/L, hemoglobin A1c 7.4%. Vitals that day: temperature 36.8 C, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, oxygen saturation 97% on room air, blood pressure 142/86 mmHg.

Assessment: the ankle swelling can come from the prednisone itself, from a rheumatoid flare, or less often from a clot. A Wells score of 1 puts the clot risk in the low range, so no lower-extremity duplex ultrasound is planned [presidio-date-time]. No arthrocentesis and no joint injection are planned either.

Plan: we are sending a referral to Pain Clinic for the chronic joint pain and a referral to Diabetes Center so the metformin dose can be reviewed against the A1c. Cardiology does not need a new visit. [presidio-person] is not indicated unless the skin opens. Please send a portal update in [presidio-date-time] with a repeat home blood pressure and whether the ankle still will not take a shoe. If the joint becomes hot, you cannot bear weight, or you have chest pain or sudden shortness of breath, go to urgent care [presidio-date-time] rather than waiting on this thread.

All eight sites show distorted crypt architecture, basal plasmacytosis,

Colon, cecum through rectum, biopsies: chronic colitis, mildly active
in the distal samples, inactive in the proximal samples. Negative for
dysplasia and negative for carcinoma.

DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Principal diagnosis: aspiration pneumonia, improved, with a concurrent exacerbation of chronic obstructive pulmonary disease.
Additional diagnoses: Parkinson disease, oropharyngeal dysphagia, and allergic rhinitis.
Disposition: home with his son after swallow teaching. A referral was placed to speech therapy and to pulmonology as outpatient services.

History of present illness. The patient is a [presidio-date-time] man who came in with [presidio-date-time] of fever, productive cough, and a choking spell while drinking water. Parkinson disease was diagnosed in [presidio-date-time] and has caused a soft voice, a shuffling gait, and slowing of his swallow. A videofluoroscopic swallow study in [presidio-date-time] showed delayed initiation and silent aspiration of thin liquids. He had been eating in bed. His son, who is 44 and lives nearby, noticed milder confusion than the patient's usual baseline and brought him in.

Past history. COPD has been present since [presidio-date-time], with two exacerbations treated with steroids in [presidio-date-time], though not with intubation. Allergic rhinitis is longstanding and is the reason he keeps Allegra at home. There is no heart failure, no prior stroke, and no gastrointestinal bleeding. He stopped tobacco [presidio-date-time]. Home medicines were carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg PO TID, tiotropium 18 mcg inhaled once daily, fluticasone-salmeterol 250/50 one inhalation BID, Allegra 180 mg PO [presidio-date-time], and aspirin 81 mg PO [presidio-date-time]. He has no known drug allergy. The brand Allegra and the generic fexofenadine were both listed on old bottles, and only one was continued.

Examination and data. Temperature 38.4 C, blood pressure 128/72 mmHg, heart rate 104 beats per minute, respiratory rate 24 breaths per minute, and oxygen saturation 88 percent on room air, improving to 95 percent on 3 liters by nasal cannula. Crackles were heard at the right base. The examination fit Parkinson disease, with resting tremor, rigidity, and a stooped posture, and there was no new hemiparesis. White blood cell count 16.2 thousand per microliter, hemoglobin 13.4 g/dL, platelets 210 thousand per microliter, sodium 133 mmol/L, potassium 3.8 mmol/L, creatinine 1.0 mg/dL, glucose 142 mg/dL, and lactate 1.4 mmol/L. Procalcitonin was 0.8 ng/[presidio-person] radiograph showed a right lower lobe infiltrate without a large effusion. Blood cultures were sent before antibiotics.

Hospital course. He was transfered from the emergency department to the ward on supplemental oxygen. [presidio-date-time] g IV q24h and azithromycin 500 mg IV [presidio-date-time] were begun for pneumonia. Azithromycin was stopped when the legionella antigen came back negative, and ceftriaxone was changed to amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg PO BID to complete [presidio-date-time]. Prednisone was given as 40/30/20/10 mg PO [presidio-date-time] for the COPD flare, [presidio-date-time] at each step, with food. Glucose stayed under 180 mg/dL without insulin. A bedside swallow evaluation was followed by a repeat videofluoroscopic swallow study, wich confirmed ongoing risk with thin liquids and safer handling of nectar-thick liquids and soft solids. Speech therapy practiced chin tuck and smaller bites. Oxygen was weaned to room air, and resting saturation stayed stabel at 94 percent. He walked with a walker and standby assist. Carbidopa-levodopa was kept on the home schedule. The covering pharmacist stopped the duplicate fexofenadine so that Allegra 180 mg PO [presidio-date-time] was the only antihistamine. We reccomend that the son set out the levodopa doses and watch the [presidio-date-time] meal.

Discharge medications.
Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875 mg PO BID for [presidio-date-time] of a [presidio-date-time] course.
Prednisone 40/30/20/10 mg PO [presidio-date-time], [presidio-date-time] at each step, then stop.
Carbidopa-levodopa 25/100 mg PO TID.
Tiotropium 18 mcg inhaled once [presidio-date-time].
Fluticasone-salmeterol 250/50 mcg one inhalation BID.
Allegra 180 mg PO [presidio-date-time]. Do not also take fexofenadine.
Aspirin 81 mg PO [presidio-date-time].
Albuterol 2 puffs inhaled [presidio-date-time] as needed for wheeze.
Acetaminophen 650 mg PO [presidio-date-time] as needed for fever.

Follow-up and precautions. He should return for worse dyspnea, new fever, chest pain, or confusion that comes back. Liquids at home should stay nectar-thick until speech therapy says otherwise. Meals are best taken upright, with no lying back for [presidio-date-time]. His son will stay [presidio-date-time] for the first several nights. Pulmonology follow-up is requested to review whether the inhaled combination should continue, and neurology follow-up is requested for the Parkinson disease medicines. The instructions were read back by the patient and his son.

Signed by the discharging hospitalist for the inpatient team.

TELEPHONE ENCOUNTER TRANSCRIPT
DEPARTMENT: AMBULATORY CARE PHARMACY AND CLINICAL TRIAGE
COMMUNICATION TYPE: POST-DISCHARGE RECONCILIATION AND CARE COORDINATION
STATUS: ROUTINE ENCOUNTER

TRIAGE NURSE: Good morning, clinical triage line. This is the triage nurse on duty. How can I assist pharmacy [presidio-date-time]?

COVERING PHARMACIST: Hello, good morning. This is the covering pharmacist from the outpatient clinical team. I am calling to review the transition of care orders and discharge documentation recieved from Outside Hospital for a [presidio-date-time] patient who was recently evaluated for acute unilateral facial paralysis and diagnosed with Bell palsy. The clinical notes also noted pre-existing focal neuropathic pain diagnosed in [presidio-date-time]. I noticed a few discrepancies on the discharge medication reconciliation and wanted to clarify the dosing schedule and prior authorization status with the clinical team before sending the maintenance prescriptions through for dispensing.

TRIAGE NURSE: Thank you for following up on this. I have teh scanned chart and the consultation packet from Outside Hospital open in front of me right now. The patient was initially evaluated in the emergency department and then admitted to the clinical observation unit before being discharged home in stable condition. What specific questions did you have regarding the medication regimen?

COVERING PHARMACIST: First, regarding the systemic steroid therapy for the acute Bell palsy. The inpatient team initiated an oral corticosteroid taper, but the discharge summary and the electronic discharge order transmitted to the pharmacy contained conflicting directions. The written discharge summary recommended a standard prednisone 60/40/20/10 mg taper over [presidio-date-time], but the electronic order was entered as prednisone 40 mg PO [presidio-date-time] for [presidio-date-time] without tapering instructions. Given the severity of the facial weakness at presentation, the standard clinical protocol recommends the higher initial dose burst followed by a gradual reduction: prednisone 60 mg PO [presidio-date-time] for [presidio-date-time], then 40 mg PO [presidio-date-time] for [presidio-date-time], 20 mg PO [presidio-date-time] for [presidio-date-time], and 10 mg PO [presidio-date-time] for [presidio-date-time]. Has the attending physician confirmed which taper schedule we should follow?

TRIAGE NURSE: Yes, let me look at the clinical addendum entered [presidio-date-time]. The attending physician reviewed the outside records and confirmed that the prednisone 60/40/20/10 mg taper is indeed the intended course. In addition, the current orders include valacyclovir 1000 mg PO TID for [presidio-date-time] for antiviral coverage, plus preservative-free artificial tears 1 drop in the right eye q2h PRN while awake, and lubricating ophthalmic ointment 0.25 inch to the right eye at bedtime. Because the patient cannot achieve full right eyelid closure, corneal protection is critical right now.

COVERING PHARMACIST: Excellent, that provides clear direction on the acute regimen. Next, I wanted to address the neuropathic pain therapy. According to the medical history dating back to [presidio-date-time], the patient has chronic peripheral neuropathy. During the observation stay, the inpatient team started Lyrica 75 mg PO BID. However, the pre-admission medication profile still includes gabapentin 300 mg PO TID. This represents dual gabapentinoid therapy. Combining Lyrica and gabapentin creates an unnecessary risk of additive central nervous system depression, marked somnolence, dizziness, and peripheral edema. My clinical recommendation is to discontinue the outpatient gabapentin completely and continue the Lyrica monotherapy, titrating upward as tolerated.

TRIAGE NURSE: That makes total sense. I will submit an order modification to discontinue gabapentin 300 mg PO TID and keep Lyrica 75 mg PO BID as the single agent for neuropathic pain. The primary care provider also placed an electronic referral to Pain Clinic for comprehensive multidisciplinary evaluation once the steroid taper is completed. Has the patient's health plan cleared the Lyrica prescription, or will an appeal be required?

COVERING PHARMACIST: The electronic pharmacy adjudication system initially rejected the prescription claim, requesting prior authorization due to formulary step-therapy requirements. However, because the historical records confirm documented trials and therapeutic failure of both gabapentin and duloxetine since [presidio-date-time], we have strong justification. I am preparing the prior authorization appeal documentation right now. Could you please share the most recent vital signs and laboratory findings from the clinical records so I can attach them to the justification package?

TRIAGE NURSE: Absolutely. At the discharge evaluation, vital signs were documented as follows: blood pressure 126/82 mmHg, heart rate 70 bpm, respiratory rate 16 breaths per minute, body temperature 98.4 F, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The patient was alert, oriented, and experiencing no systemic symtoms. Laboratory results from the hospital admission were: fasting blood glucose 106 mg/dL, hemoglobin A1c 5.9%, serum sodium 140 mEq/L, serum potassium 4.2 mEq/L, blood urea nitrogen 15 mg/dL, serum creatinine 0.84 mg/dL, estimated glomerular filtration rate 96 mL/min/1.73 [presidio-us-driver-license], aspartate aminotransferase 24 U/L, alanine aminotransferase 28 U/L, and complete blood count showing a white blood cell count of 7.8 [presidio-us-driver-license]^3/uL, hemoglobin 14.1 g/dL, and platelet count 245 [presidio-us-driver-license]^3/uL. Renal and hepatic parameters are completely normal, so no dose adjustment is necessary for Lyrica.

COVERING PHARMACIST: Those laboratory values are very helpful and support the clinical need. Were there any diagnostic imaging studies or specialty procedures completed during the hospitalization?

TRIAGE NURSE: Yes. Diagnostic magnetic resonance imaging of the brain and internal auditory canal with intravenous gadolinium contrast was performed at Outside Hospital. The radiologist reported prominent enhancement of the right facial nerve within the geniculate ganglion and tympanic segments, entirely consistent with acute Bell palsy, without evidence of intracranial mass, acute ischemia, or vascular compression. High-resolution computed tomography of the temporal bone showed clear mastoid air cells and intact bony architecture. The neurology consultant documented a House-Brackmann score of grade [presidio-nrp] facial paresis and advised follow-up electromyography in [presidio-date-time] if clinical recovery is delayed.

COVERING PHARMACIST: Perfect. I will assemble the prior authorization request with the clinical summary, imaging reports, and renal panel, and submit it directly to the health plan. In the meantime, I will dispense the prednisone 60/40/20/10 mg taper, valacyclovir 1000 mg PO TID, and the ocular lubricants for immediate courier delivery so there is no delay in treating the Bell palsy.

TRIAGE NURSE: Thank you so much for your thorough review and for streamlining this transition. I will alert the primary care team and place a note in the electronic chart. Have a wonderful rest of your shift.

COVERING PHARMACIST: You too. Thank you, goodbye.
